item.title: Edge0-145B: Frontier AI Capabilities on Your Own Computer
item.abstract:
Today, we're open-sourcing Edge0-145B and Edge0-120B , together with our unified inference framework and deployment tools. Edge0-145B is the world's first open-source on-device AI model with 145 billion parameters. It brings coding, reasoning, and agent capabilities that rival frontier cloud models to your own computer. On-device AI has long forced a tradeoff between model capability and what the hardware can run. Larger models demand more memory, bandwidth, and power; smaller models can struggle with complex work. Moving that work to the cloud adds model-provider fees, data-handling constraints, and a dependence on connectivity. This release addresses those constraints in four ways: The constraint What Edge0-145B makes possible Large models are difficult to run on personal hardware. A 145B model runs locally on a compatible laptop, with reported peak memory of 29GB and decoding above 80 tokens/s. Small on-device models can fall short on demanding tasks. Coding, reasoning, and instruction-following results are competitive with specific frontier cloud models, as the comparisons below show. A useful assistant needs to finish work, not just answer questions. The model plans, writes and runs code, debugs errors, and checks results visually for projects such as 3D scenes, games, hardware programs, and PCB designs. Cloud workflows bring recurring fees, sensitive-data restrictions, and network dependence. Local inference incurs no corresponding cloud-model token or API fees; data can stay on the computer, and core capabilities keep working offline. Hardware and electricity still cost money. We're releasing the full stack so developers can reproduce the results, evaluate or fine-tune the models, and integrate them into their own products. Get the model weights , explore the inference framework , or try the Edge0 App . How We Make 100B+ Parameter AI Run on a Personal Computer Edge0-145B Laptop Performance: Memory, Speed, and Power Edge0-145B makes a 145-billion-parameter model usable on a personal laptop. A useful local model has to fit in memory, process prompts promptly, generate fast enough to use, and keep power consumption under control. It also needs to sustain longer tasks. Requirement Reported Edge0-145B result What it enables Memory 29GB peak memory Runs on a compatible personal laptop, such as a MacBook Pro, without a server. Prompt processing 1,100+ tokens/s prefill Processes long prompts, including dozens of pages of code, before generation begins. Generation 80+ tokens/s decode Generates faster than a person reads. Power Approximately 120W typical power Sustains operation without throttling in the reported setup. Long tasks 128K–256K context Maintains essentially the same speed on long inputs, supporting extended work. Our earlier Edge0-35B phone release reported peak memory below 2.5GB. On an iPhone 18 Pro Max, Edge0-35B delivers 37+ tokens/s using approximately 2.5GB of memory. Edge0-145B has roughly four times as many parameters; its laptop comparison reports 80+ tokens/s and 28GB peak memory. These measurements apply to different models and hardware. On-device model scale over time. The chart covers 67 open models of at least 1B parameters from 14 labs, intended for phones, laptops, and AI PCs. Same-size base, instruct, and reasoning variants count once; each line tracks a lab's largest model, including releases before July 2025. Filled points mark new highs and hollow points other releases. The scale is logarithmic below 40B and linear above it. Apple is excluded because its weights are not released. Sources: vendor announcements and model cards. Why On-Device Models Have Stayed Small Memory limits kept most on-device models below 10B parameters before September 2026. Apple Intelligence's on-device foundation model had approximately 3B parameters, while Google's Gemini Nano came in 1.8B and 3.25B versions. Even a 7B model could consume approximately 4GB of memory. Larger models faced a memory wall. Model weights occupy storage and must be read during generation, competing for limited memory and bandwidth with the operating system and other apps. Even an aggressively compressed 35B model could need approximately 20GB of memory, far more than a phone could make available. Compute, bandwidth, and power created competing constraints. Larger models offered more capability, but strained memory capacity, generation speed, and battery life. Making models smaller helped them fit, often at the cost of capability. Privacy alone could not close that gap. Apple Intelligence protected user data, but Apple acknowledged that its on-device model was not designed for agentic applications requiring general world knowledge. The prevailing assumption was that on-device intelligence could not match the cloud. Under the Hood of Edge0: Four Layers of Model and Inference Design We designed Edge0-145B and its inference engine together to reduce the memory and data movement that make large models difficult to run locally. The design spans architecture, training, loading, and scheduling. Architecture: share large matrices across sparse experts. Sharing matrices substantially reduces the weights that must be stored and moved while keeping the expert count unchanged. Each group of 64 experts shares two large matrices, while each expert retains a small set of parameters that captures its differences. Previously, every expert stored a complete set of matrices. Of the model's 145B total parameters, only approximately 10B participate in computation on each inference step. Training: build for local execution from day one. We train the model in its on-device architecture from the outset, with deployment constraints built into its design. This avoids treating local deployment as a compression or pruning step after training a cloud model. Loading: pipeline GPU memory, system memory, and SSD access. Reading and computation overlap across three storage tiers, avoiding serial waits. Frequently used “hot experts” remain in GPU memory. An expert library of approximately 40GB sits in system memory, with experts brought into GPU memory as needed. Approximately 48GB of vocabulary data resides on the SSD and is read on demand. Scheduling: use the CPU and GPU together. The GPU computes cached experts while the CPU handles the remaining work in parallel. Speculative decoding verifies multiple candidate tokens at once, spreading the cost of reading weights across more output tokens. These choices support the reported 80+ tokens/s decode rate. Model and inference-engine design work together to make 100B+ parameter inference practical on personal computers. Source: internal testing. Together, these changes let parameter counts grow from tens of billions to more than a hundred billion without proportional increases in memory use, power consumption, and latency. What Edge0 Can Do: Anything From Chat to Complex Work on Your Computer Edge0-145B can carry a complex task through to a usable result. Its coding and reasoning capabilities support local workflows that combine planning, tool use, execution, debugging, and visual checks. The benchmarks establish its capabilities; the demonstrations show how it puts them to work. Coding and reasoning that rival frontier cloud models Edge0-145B is competitive with specific frontier cloud models across coding, reasoning, knowledge, and instruction following: Coding: It scores 64.6 on DeepSWE 1.1 , ahead of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next at 58.7 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 at 54.4. Reasoning and knowledge: It scores 90.4 on GPQA-Diamond , close to DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 at 90.8 and Claude-Opus-4.6 \(Max\) at 91.3. Instruction following: It scores 80.6 on IFBench , ahead of DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 at 79.2 and Claude-Opus-4.6 \(Max\) at 62.5. Its 86.52 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 also exceeds Qwen3.8-Flash-Next's 83.3, DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731's 82.7, and Claude's 78.2. On AA-LCR, Edge0-145B scores 79.3 to Claude's 78.0.

item.title: Google Releases TPU Sync: Open-Source KV Cache Transfer for TPUs
item.abstract: Google Cloud has released TPU Sync , an open-source C++ library for moving KV caches and model weights on Cloud TPUs. The Google TPU Sync KV cache transfer library treats TPU HBM, host DRAM, shared storage and the data center network as one memory hierarchy. It targets a growing bottleneck: moving model state, not computing it. Google reports over 90% lower KV transfer latency on 235B to 480B parameter MoE models. TPU Sync is an open-source C++ library from Google that moves TPU-tiled tensors across memory tiers with asynchronous DMA. It handles 2 jobs: KV cache state during inference, and trainer-to-sampler weight broadcast in reinforcement learning (RL). The repository is licensed Apache-2.0. The library spans TPU HBM, pinned host DRAM, shared storage and multi-host DCN. Storage uses experimental POSIX backends, including local SSDs and Google Cloud Managed Lustre. Google lists 4 design choices: Above this sit a global KV store for prefix lookups, a transfer controller and a KV cache manager. The prefill node offloads KV blocks to pinned host RAM through async DMA. The controller streams them host-to-host to the assigned decode node. Arriving blocks move into decode-node HBM while decoding continues. Google ran internal tests in July 2026 on TPU v7x (2x2x1). The stack was tpu-inference v0.24.0, JAX 0.10.2 and libtpu 0.0.42.1. Google team states that real-world results will vary. For P/D disaggregated serving: TPU Sync integrates with PyTorch through TorchTPU and with JAX natively. In vLLM-TorchTPU , it is the TPU KV connector behind vLLM’s KVConnector interface. In SGLang-TorchTPU , it is the P/D transfer backend and hierarchical cache I/O backend. On GKE, llm-d 1.0 uses it for prefix-cache-affinity routing and experimental spill to Managed Lustre. Inferact and RadixArk co-engineered the vLLM and SGLang integrations. Google says Meta and Wayfair are evaluating the architecture. The bandwidth figures measure different paths. TPU Sync’s number is host PCIe DMA. Mooncake’s number is network transfer over RoCE. Check out the technical blog , the GitHub repo , vLLM-TorchTPU and SGLang-TorchTPU . item.title: Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Orchestrator
item.abstract:
0:00 / 0:00 Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Orchestrator - Blog blog Blog Blog Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Orchestrator - Blog Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Orchestrator The Antigravity Team · Nov 12, 2026 · 3 min read Today, we’re rolling out Gemini 4 Hydrogen inside Google Antigravity alongside a new model dropdown option called Orchestrator, which pairs Hydrogen with our strongest models for long-horizon tasks, including Gemini 4 Carbon, in an optimized balance of quality, efficiency, and latency. Selecting Orchestrator (Carbon) from the model selector in Google Antigravity. Put Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen to work with Orchestrator Earlier this week, we introduced Gemini 4 Carbon alongside /swarm for tackling massive, multi-worktree engineering tasks with parallel agent teams. In just a couple of days, tens of thousands of swarms have been launched on Antigravity, pushing frontier intelligence on the hardest problems. For everyday feature work and debugging inside a single session, running a frontier reasoning model with multiple parallel agents on every step of every routine task slows down your loop and burns frontier quota. A common industry approach is to use a static “model router” that guesses task difficulty from your first prompt and routes the entire task to the cheapest model that is good enough to complete the task. Unfortunately, these start breaking down as agents become longer running, requiring different levels of complexity at different stages, often discovered as the task evolves. Orchestrator takes a dynamic, bidirectional approach between Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen within the evolution of a single trajectory. For example, Carbon can start in a read-only phase to explore dependencies, resolve ambiguities, and build a concrete plan with explicit re-planning triggers. Hydrogen could then take over to write edits, update packages, and run tests. If Hydrogen hits friction, it would hand back to Carbon to inspect the state, repair the plan, and resume execution. This allows Orchestrator to reach near-Carbon task success while being faster and more quota-efficient. On Terminal-Bench 4.1, Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while, on average, consuming 24% less quota and completing 19% faster. Explicit multi-model pipelines with the Antigravity SDK: When you want programmatic control over which model handles each role, you can wire Hydrogen and Carbon together directly with the Antigravity SDK. In the demo below, an open-source issue triage system built with the Antigravity SDK pairs multiple agents together. The Hydrogen agents handle triaging and coding to keep up with incoming issue volume, searching the codebase, asking clarifying questions, and fast UI iteration from PR comments while the Carbon agent is assigned to larger refactors, new features, and security checks. Pairing Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Gemini 4 Carbon with the Antigravity SDK for automated open-source issue triage and code generation. Fast, dependable execution with Gemini 4 Hydrogen: Hydrogen also works as a standalone model for everyday coding and agentic work, scoring 51 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (surpassing Argon’s 50, and reaching 54 at its highest setting) and 57% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 (more than tripiling 3.8 Flash’s 18.2%). When selecting Hydrogen directly, you can dial reasoning depth across four thinking levels, low, medium, high (default), and a new xhigh tier. Using Gemini 4 Hydrogen in Google Antigravity to upgrade dependencies, refactor shared utilities, and generate accessible image alt text. Getting started Gemini 4 Hydrogen brings cutting-edge intelligence for everyday coding and agentic workflows. When you want frontier planning paired with speed without managing model switches, Orchestrator puts both Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen behind one prompt. Starting today, Gemini 4 Hydrogen is rolling out across paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. Orchestrator is rolling out as Orchestrator (Carbon) and Orchestrator (Argon) for Google AI Ultra subscribers, and as Orchestrator (Argon) for paid Google AI Pro subscribers, with additional models and plans supported in the future. Enterprises can access both in Gemini for business . Download Antigravity Read the Orchestrator docs

item.title: Google Releases Gemini 4 Hydrogen: 2.5x Faster Than Gemini 3.8 Flash
item.abstract: Google has released Gemini 4 Hydrogen , a fast model for coding and agentic work. Gemini 4 Hydrogen is a proprietary model from Google DeepMind built for everyday agent loops. It sits below the frontier models Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon . Google calls it its “daily driver for agentic workflows.” Hydrogen is a closed-weights model served through the Gemini API and Google products. The model card says it is adapted from Gemini 4 Carbon. Google does not disclose parameter count, architecture or training hardware. The knowledge cutoff is March 2026. Input covers text, images, audio, video, PDFs, tables and charts, per the What’s New guide . Output is text. The 1M window is shared by input, thinking and output tokens. Developers set thinking_level inside generation_config . Values are low , medium , high and a new xhigh . The default is high , not medium as on 3.8 Flash. A minimal setting now returns an error. The model card warns that higher levels use more tokens. The key design idea is role-splitting across models. In Google Antigravity , an Orchestrator option switches models inside 1 task. Carbon explores, resolves ambiguity and plans. Hydrogen edits files, updates packages and runs tests. When Hydrogen hits friction, it hands control back to Carbon. On Terminal-Bench 4.1, this pairing reached near-Carbon task success rates. It used 24% less quota and finished 19% faster than Carbon alone. The Antigravity SDK exposes the same split for custom multi-agent systems. All figures are self-reported by Google unless noted. Speed is the headline claim. Hydrogen finishes tasks 2.5x faster than 3.8 Flash at the default high level. In partner tests, it ran 2x to 2.8x faster with 12% to 23% fewer tokens. Google also reports more than 5x fewer fabricated claims than 3.8 Flash. It scored 96.7% on an internal agent honesty evaluation. It was 2.3x more resilient to indirect prompt injection on Gray Swan’s benchmark. The API price is $1.50 per 1M input tokens and $7.50 per 1M output tokens. Pricing is flat across the full window. Output pricing includes thinking tokens. Implicit caching cuts input to $0.075 per 1M for prompts of 4,096 tokens or more. Explicit caching is not supported. The price context matters. Gemini 3.8 Flash costs $0.75/$3.75 until December 31, 2026. From January 1, 2027, it rises to $1.50/$7.50, matching Hydrogen. Argon costs $2/$10 until November 30, 2026, then $4/$20. The model ID is gemini-4-hydrogen . It is live in the Gemini API, Google AI Studio on all tiers, and Android Studio. It also ships in Gemini for business , the Gemini app, Google Search and Sheets. Antigravity access requires Google AI Pro or Ultra. Vertex AI is not mentioned in the launch posts. Migration from 3.8 Flash needs a few changes. Remove temperature , top_p and top_k , since the server ignores them. Remove cached_content fields. Raise hardcoded max_output_tokens caps to 65,536. Terminal-Bench 4.0 and 4.1 are different versions, so cross-version scores are not directly comparable. Check out the launch post , the model card , the developer post and the What’s New guide . item.title: When One GPU Isn’t Enough: Serving GLM-5.3 Across Two NVIDIA DGX Stations with vLLM
item.abstract:
Running a frontier-scale model locally means keeping all its weights in GPU memory; the largest models no longer fit on one machine. Two NVIDIA DGX Stations connected over ConnectX-8 RDMA serve one model through a single endpoint, with tensor parallelism splitting the model weights and computation across both GPUs. The NVIDIA GLM-5.3 NVFP4 model, a quantized version of Z.ai ’s mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, has 753 billion parameters, with 40 billion activated per token. Sparse activation reduces computation, but all model weights still need to remain available because each token can be routed to different experts. At about 464 GB, the checkpoint exceeds the 252 GB of HBM3e on a single GB300 GPU. This tutorial uses two DGX Stations to keep the weights in GPU memory, with CPU weight offload disabled. Before starting, connect the two Stations with the Connect Two DGX Stations playbook . This post shows how to serve GLM-5.3 locally across two NVIDIA DGX Stations with vLLM, send a request, and measure behavior under concurrent load. Tensor parallelism (TP=2) splits the model’s tensors across the two GB300 GPUs. Both Stations compute every request, and Station A returns the answer through one OpenAI-compatible API. By the end, you’ll have a working endpoint and a baseline for how it behaves under load. Figure 1. Two Stations serve one model: each GPU holds and computes part of the model over the selected RDMA connection. Their memories remain distinct Prerequisites Two GB300 DGX Stations running Linux, connected and validated with the Connect Two DGX Stations playbook , including its GPU-memory RDMA test on both rails. SSH and sudo access on both Stations with the same Linux username. Docker and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit come preinstalled with the DGX Station software stack . Allow outbound access to the container registry, Hugging Face, and package repositories. At least 464 GB of free disk space on each Station for its copy of the checkpoint, plus room for the vLLM container image and temporary files. Acceptance of the NVIDIA Open Model Agreement and the original GLM-5.3 license terms, listed on the model card . SPEED-Bench is governed by the NVIDIA Evaluation Dataset License Agreement . A Hugging Face account and read access token, with access to the gated cais/hle dataset: sign in, open its page, and select Agree and access repository . Step 5 downloads SPEED-Bench prompts from this dataset. The companion video follows the same workflow. Video 1. Walkthrough of preparation, inference, benchmarking, and shutdown Step 1. Alternatively, work from a local terminal on each Station. The docker group grants root-level privileges. The ibdev2netdev output lists the two direct rails, cx8r0 and cx8r1 . “你換個統計口徑，這個顯著規律還在嗎？” 很多時候，所謂的“重大發現”，只是恰好卡在某個特定的篩選閾值上。要驗證結論硬不硬，研究員得推翻重篩樣本、調整納入標準、重跑全套檢驗。 在一道乳腺癌臨床佇列任務（BiomniBench da-18-7）中，任務要求探究內分泌治療後的HR+/HER2−乳腺癌患者體內，ESR1突變與RAS/MAPK通路變異到底是“傾向共存”還是“相互排斥”。 item.title: Chinese frontier AI models carry the fingerprint of export-controlled GPUs
item.abstract:
Top Chinese Frontier AI Models Carry the Fingerprint of Export-Controlled NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs Will DePue November 12, 2026 Print / save PDF Cite this report Executive Summary Our forensic analysis of publicly released AI models finds evidence that DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group have gained access to NVIDIA’s Blackwell GPUs, despite restrictions on exporting these chips to China, and are using that hardware to create their AI models. Six models released by these companies since April 2026 contain numerical patterns matching Blackwell hardware, whereas earlier models from the same companies match NVIDIA’s older Hopper generation. The findings suggest that several leading Chinese AI developers have begun using Blackwell to train their newest models. U.S. officials and press reports had already alleged that DeepSeek and Moonshot AI were using Blackwell chips, without publishing technical evidence. The evidence comes entirely from the models’ own published weights, rather than from leaks or insider accounts. We recover traces of the models’ initial values, and then search for the hardware configurations and initial configurations that reproduce them; for DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Kimi K3, we also confirmed the match on physical Blackwell chips. The fingerprint identifies how the weights were created and supports, without proving, the inference that Blackwell also performed the training. Specially configured AMD hardware, which is also restricted from export to China, is the only alternative we have identified; we have excluded it for DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and consider it very unlikely for the other five models. Notably, our findings provide technical evidence of access to advanced computing hardware, but do not establish where the chips were located, how access was obtained, or whether export controls were violated. Table 1. Hardware fingerprints in successive models from DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group Link ↗ Lab Model Released Chip the model was started on DeepSeek DeepSeek-V3 Dec 2024 NVIDIA Hopper (lab disclosed H800) DeepSeek-V4-Flash Apr 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell B200/B300 DeepSeek-V4-Pro Apr 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell GB200/GB300 Moonshot AI Kimi K2 Jul 2025 NVIDIA Hopper (lab disclosed H800) Kimi K2.5 Jan 2026 NVIDIA Hopper (lab disclosed H800) Kimi K3 Jul 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell GB200/GB300 Kimi K3.1-Pro Nov 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell GB200/GB300 MiniMax MiniMax-M2.7 Apr 2026 NVIDIA Hopper MiniMax-M3 Jun 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell B200/B300 Ant Group Ling-3.0-flash Aug 2026 NVIDIA Hopper Ling-3.1-flash Oct 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell GB200/GB300 • Requires a U.S. license for export to China; none have been reported. A Hopper fingerprint cannot distinguish an H800 from an H100 SXM or H200; the H800 identifications above are lab disclosures, not findings of this method. Full list of models in Appendix 2 ↓ Main Findings Six models from four Chinese labs read as Blackwell-trained. DeepSeek-V4-Flash and MiniMax-M3 match NVIDIA’s Blackwell-class B200 or B300 chips, which have 148 processor cores (called streaming multiprocessors , or SMs). DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, Kimi K3.1-Pro and Ling-3.1-flash match the GB200 or GB300 chips, also Blackwell-class, which have 152 processor cores. Kimi K3.1-Pro starts from the same seed as K3, and may be a checkpoint of K3 with further post-training. Chinese labs started training on Blackwell relatively recently. DeepSeek’s models read as Hopper-trained through DeepSeek-V3 (released in December 2024), and as Blackwell from DeepSeek V4 (released in April 2026). Moonshot’s models read as Hopper through Kimi K2.5 (January 2026) and as Blackwell from K3 (July 2026). One Moonshot model sits in between: Kimi K2.7-Code, posted six weeks before K3, is built on the Hopper-era weights but contains a small part that matches the B200 or B300. MiniMax’s models read as Hopper through M2.7 (April 2026) and as Blackwell from M3 (June 2026). Ant Group’s Ling-3.0-flash (August 2026) reads as Hopper, while its Ling-3.1-flash (October 2026) reads as Blackwell. The Hopper readings do not identify a specific chip: H800s, H100 SXMs and H200s share the same fingerprint. Not every Chinese AI lab has switched to Blackwell. The newest models we could read from Alibaba (Qwen), Zhipu (GLM), Tencent, Xiaomi and StepFun all read as Hopper-trained. Meituan says its LongCat-2.0 was trained entirely on “AI ASIC superpods,” and we found no NVIDIA fingerprint in the model weights it’s released. The method gets known answers right. For 24 specific models, the developer has publicly said what hardware was used. In every case, our method agrees with the public announcement. NVIDIA’s own Nemotron-3 Ultra, whose technical report names the GB200 for one phase of its training, reads as 152 SMs, the same as Kimi K3. The matches are far stronger than chance would explain. Even unrelated numbers can appear to match when enough combinations are tried. Across the roughly 6 trillion seed-and-layout combinations in our search, the strongest chance match would be expected to reach about 8 sigma—a measure of how far a result stands above ordinary random variation. The strongest evidence for each of the six models ranges from 49 to 1,385 sigma. Even the weakest individual test we report reaches 20 sigma. The training runs were data-center scale. From each model’s size and the amount of data it was trained on, we estimate that the two largest runs, Kimi K3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, each needed thousands of Blackwell GPUs for two to three months, assuming each model was trained on the hardware that initialized it. Our best estimates are about 4,500 and 3,000, the equivalent of about 11,500 and 7,500 H100s, the previous-generation NVIDIA chip in which AI training clusters are commonly sized, and about 12,000 Blackwell GPUs across the five runs (Table 2). At roughly $70,000 per GPU—the cost implied by a Wall Street Journal report that about 36,000 Blackwell chips being installed in Malaysia for ByteDance’s use would cost more than $2.5 billion—the largest of these clusters would cost roughly $200 million to $300 million, and the five together more than half a billion dollars. These figures cover only the final training runs; the labs’ total spending on export-controlled GPUs is likely in the billions of dollars. Table 2. Rough scale of each training run Link ↗ Model H100 equivalents Blackwell GPUs, best estimate Blackwell range Estimated run length DeepSeek-V4-Flash 3,500 1,500 250–5,000 50 days DeepSeek-V4-Pro 7,500 3,000 750–6,500 70 days Kimi K3 11,500 4,500 1,000–9,500 70 days MiniMax-M3 3,500 1,500 200–7,000 60 days Ling-3.1-flash 4,000 1,500 400–6,500 100 days All five 30,000 12,000 7,000–22,000 Each estimate is a run’s training compute divided by what one Blackwell GPU delivers over the run, rounded to the nearest 500. Training compute is about six operations per active parameter for every training token, plus attention. We assume the GPUs ran at about 20% of their peak speed, in line with other disclosed Blackwell training runs (25% for DeepSeek, which has reported 39% for its previous model), and for the run lengths shown, which we estimate from release timelines. H100 equivalents convert at NVIDIA’s published peak speeds: a B200 or B300 equals about 2.3 H100s, and a GB200 or GB300 about 2.5. We are not confident in these estimates. They rest on assumptions that the weights cannot confirm: how efficiently each lab used its GPUs (often called MFU), which no lab has published for these runs; how many tokens each model was trained on (DeepSeek’s counts are its own, and we take them on trust; the others are our estimates, made from the weights by a method we have not yet published); how long each run lasted, which no lab has stated; and that training stayed on the hardware that created the weights. Run length matters most, because halving it doubles the GPU count.

item.title: Liquid AI Releases LiquidCodec, a 74M-Parameter Streaming Audio Codec
item.abstract: Liquid AI has released LiquidCodec , the audio codec behind its LFM3-Audio-2B and LFM3-Omni-2B models. The LiquidCodec audio codec is a ~74M-parameter streaming speech tokenizer. It turns speech into tokens a language model can predict, then converts those tokens back into audio. Liquid AI had 2 goals: easy-to-predict tokens and fast conversion back to speech. The weights are on Hugging Face . LiquidCodec is a Liquid AI speech codec that compresses 24 kHz audio into 12 token streams. Each 80 ms frame becomes 12 discrete tokens, per the LFM3-Audio-2B model card . It replaces Kyutai’s Mimi , which Liquid AI used in LFM2-Audio-1.5B. Mimi has 96.2M parameters. The pipeline is encode, quantize, decode. Liquid AI uses blocks from its LFM3 architecture in both the encoder and decoder. The 2 halves are symmetric, and the encoder is fully causal, which suits streaming. Quantization uses grouped finite scalar quantization (GFSQ) instead of residual vector quantization (RVQ). In RVQ, each codebook encodes what the previous one missed. GFSQ groups are independent, so all 12 codebooks can be predicted in parallel by MaskGIT-style transformers. The decoder predicts spectral coefficients directly. This avoids learned transposed-convolution upsampling, a common cost in waveform decoders. Training ran in 2 stages. Stage 1 used 264,000 hours of speech across 107 languages. It applied waveform and spectral losses, without adversarial losses. Stage 2 fine-tuned on 55,000 hours of full-band speech (24 kHz or higher) with adversarial critics. Liquid AI says this removed metallic artifacts left after stage 1. A final decoder-only quantization-aware training (QAT) step targets edge inference. Liquid AI measured speed in FP32 on 1 CPU thread of an Apple M4 Max MacBook Pro. LiquidCodec ran at ~361x real time for encoding and ~87x for decoding. These are self-reported figures. Real-time factor (RTF) is processing time divided by audio length, so lower is better. LiquidCodec’s encode RTF is 0.0028, against 0.0361 for Mimi, 0.2145 for NanoCodec and 0.7359 for X-Codec 2. Decode RTF is 0.0115, against 0.0329, 0.2543 and 0.0379. That is about 13x lower encode RTF and 2.9x lower decode RTF than Mimi. Liquid AI used 8 test sets. These were LibriSpeech test-clean, Seed-TTS English and Mandarin, and 5 FLEURS languages (German, French, Mandarin, Japanese, Korean). item.title: Route coding agent requests to the right model on Amazon Bedrock with NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard
item.abstract: Coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenAI Codex CLI work in tasks. A developer asks for a change, and the agent reads files, edits code, and runs tests until the work is done. One task can take a few model calls or dozens. What the developer pays for is the task, not one call. The price per token alone doesn’t tell you what a whole task costs. The total depends on how many turns a model needs, how much history each turn replays, and how often a task has to be retried or never finishes. You pay for every attempt, including attempts on tasks that never finish. So when you route a coding agent’s requests between models, judge the routing by cost per solved task: the total cost of your runs divided by the number of runs whose tests pass. NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard is an open source library that helps an AI agent choose which model handles each request. You define the models that it can use and the strategy that it follows. Its LiteLLM integration supports two strategies. Stage routing reads the recent tool activity and results in the request history, and then picks one of two candidate models. Random routing picks from the configured models, with optional weights, for traffic splits and A/B comparisons. Another option you can explore is LiteLLM, who also recently shipped a native built-in Switchyard stage router as an auto-router strategy. In this post, you use the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) to deploy LiteLLM, an open source gateway for large language models (LLMs), with the Switchyard routing plugin in your AWS account. LiteLLM calls the models on Amazon Bedrock . You then use the sample’s benchmark runners to measure cost per solved task for a routed model group and for single-model baseline groups, so that you can evaluate routing against your own workloads. Note: The sample installs switchyard-server 0.3.0 from crates.io and runs the published LiteLLM v1.102.0 image. NVIDIA documents switchyard-server 0.3.0 as a demo and evaluation component, and its configuration can change between releases. This sample uses the experimental Switchyard LiteLLM integration and its configuration and APIs may change between releases. This is sample code, for non-production usage. Work with your security and legal teams to meet your organizational security, regulatory, and compliance requirements before deployment. Deploy the sample in a non-production account and test it before relying on it. Figure 1 shows the architecture of the solution. LiteLLM and the Switchyard plugin run in one container image on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on AWS Fargate , in private subnets. Figure 1: Solution architecture A request flows through these steps. The numbers match the diagram. LiteLLM listens on port 4000 in the container and is the load balancer’s target, and the task’s security group admits only the load balancer. The path allowlist keeps the LiteLLM admin UI, API docs, and key management routes unreachable. Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) holds the gateway image. AWS Secrets Manager generates the secret behind the gateway key, and the container adds the sk- prefix when it starts. The task definition passes the profile files in LITELLM_CONFIG_TEXT and SWITCHYARD_CONFIG_TEXT , and the startup script writes them to /tmp before it starts LiteLLM. Logs go to one Amazon CloudWatch log group, /<stack name>/litellm , which keeps them for 30 days, and Container Insights collects metrics. The VPC spans two Availability Zones, and one NAT gateway provides outbound access for image pulls and other AWS services. The plugin supports Stage routing, which needs exactly two candidates, and Random routing, which needs at least two and splits traffic by weight for A/B tests. Classifier-backed strategies, such as Task and Composite routing, need intermediate model calls that this integration doesn’t support. See the Switchyard routing overview for the full catalog. To follow this walkthrough, you need the following: You define the model group, configure Stage, deploy and test the gateway, and measure cost. Start by cloning the sample repository: A LiteLLM model group is one public model name with one or more deployments behind it. The sample keeps its configuration in deployment profiles under profiles/ . Each profile pairs litellm.yaml , which defines the models and gateway settings, with switchyard.toml , which controls how Switchyard picks a model. The following excerpt of profiles/stage/litellm.yaml defines the routed switchyard group, two single-model baseline groups, and the plugin registration: Both candidates share model_name: switchyard , so your client sends "model": "switchyard" and Switchyard picks a candidate. List the capable model first and the efficient model second, because Stage reads the roles from that order. The claude-opus-5-5 and nemotron-super-3-120b groups are single-model baselines. Each one always answers with its own model, so you can compare the routed group’s cost and pass rate with each model alone in the same deployment. The Stage plugin alone rejects a group without two candidates, so the image registers a small wrapper, switchyard_gateway.configured.ROUTING_PLUGIN . It applies Switchyard to groups with two or more unique candidates and passes single-model groups through. The configuration registers the wrapper twice: to pick the model and to apply the request changes that Switchyard records. Every model uses bedrock/converse/<id> , so every candidate goes through the Amazon Bedrock Converse API, and validation rejects any other route. The LiteLLM request_timeout of 600 seconds matches the load balancer’s 10-minute idle timeout. The file holds no credentials. LiteLLM reads the gateway key from the environment, and the task role supplies the AWS credentials. Never add credentials such as aws_access_key_id , aws_secret_access_key , or api_key under litellm_params : the stack copies the whole litellm.yaml into the task definition and the AWS CloudFormation template in plain text. The stack derives the task role’s Amazon Bedrock permissions from this file. For a global cross-Region inference profile, the foundation-model resource uses a * Region and a trailing * , so it also matches other model IDs with the same prefix. Review the derived policy before you deploy. The global. prefix marks a global cross-Region inference profile , and Amazon Bedrock might process those requests in supported commercial AWS Regions worldwide. If processing location matters, use a geographic profile or an in-Region model ID instead. For Nemotron 3 Super, the profile uses the in-Region model ID nvidia.nemotron-super-3-120b , which you can switch for any model for testing. Switchyard reads its algorithm and settings from switchyard.toml . The default profile, profiles/stage/switchyard.toml , configures Stage: Stage also accepts optional handoff notes and per-tier system prompts ( escalation_note , deescalation_note , capable_system_prompt , and efficient_system_prompt ). The sample profile sets none of them. For an A/B test, the Random profile in profiles/random/ uses the same models with algorithm = "random" and weights = [0.5, 0.5] , one weight per unique candidate in declaration order. To deploy it, add -c routingProfile=random to the cdk diff and cdk deploy commands in Step 3. The stack validates both files together when it synthesizes, and the preflight script runs the same checks. To check a profile change on its own, without AWS calls, run npm run validate:profile -- stage . Invalid settings stop LiteLLM when it starts, and unsupported message shapes fail before inference. You can try the gateway on your machine before you deploy anything. Docker Compose builds the same image and reads the same profile files that the stack deploys to Amazon ECS. Run from the repository root: The key that you export takes precedence over the placeholder in .env , so Compose and the smoke test use the same one.

item.title: Best AI Video Generation Models in 2026: Elo, Price per Second, Open Weights
item.abstract: The AI video leaderboard looks very different from 12 months ago. Native audio is now table stakes. Clips run 15–30 seconds. And an open-weights model sits in the top 3. This ranking (as of Nov 13, 2026) uses one quality signal: blind human-preference Elo from the Artificial Analysis Video Arena . We pair it with API price per second and the license status of the weights. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . Quality : Artificial Analysis ranks models by Elo from blind pairwise votes by validated evaluators . Each vote compares 2 clips from the same prompt. We rank by the AA-Video-T2V v2.1 (with audio) board. We also report the AA-Video-I2V v2.1 score. Anchor : Kling 3.0 1080p (Pro) is fixed at 1000 Elo on both boards. A score below 1000 means voters preferred Kling 3.0 more often. Price : Artificial Analysis lists cost per minute on each creator’s API. It normalizes to 1080p where offered. We divide by 60 to get price per second. Vendor rates at 720p are often lower, and we flag those gaps. Confidence : Most top-10 scores carry a ±13 to ±15 Elo interval. Models within ~25 points are statistically close. Treat ranks 3–8 as a cluster, not a strict order. Source: Artificial Analysis T2V and I2V leaderboards, retrieved November 13, 2026. $/sec = AA per-minute price ÷ 60. “H3 post-train” means the model was fine-tuned from MiniMax H3’s weights. Wan 3.0 holds the top text-to-video spot with 7,651 votes behind it. Alibaba launched it on August 24, 2026 . It generates 30-second 1080p clips from text, PDFs and slide decks, priced at $0.20 per second. The document-to-video input is the differentiator. You can hand it a deck and get a structured video back. The trade-off is openness. There are no downloadable weights for Wan 3.0 . Wan 2.2 (July 2025) remains Alibaba’s last open video flagship . Note the I2V gap too: Wan 3.0 drops to 11th on image-to-video. Best for: long single takes, explainer videos from existing documents. Utopai X is the only model in the top 2 on both boards. Utopai Studios, a Mountain View film studio, built it by post-training MiniMax H3 . It beats the base H3 it came from. Access runs only through Utopai’s PAI platform. PAI charges 93 credits per second , with plans starting at $15 for 1,000 credits. Developers cannot call it from a pipeline. Best for: filmmakers working inside a studio tool. Not for programmatic use. H3 is the first open-weights model in the video top tier. MiniMax launched the API on July 31, 2026 and published weights on August 3 . It is a 33B dense single-stream Transformer, using Qwen3-VL-32B as its encoder . It outputs video with native 32 kHz stereo audio. Read the license before you download. The Hugging Face weights carry real limits: Even so, H3 has become the base layer of 2026 video. Utopai X, HeyGen Video 1, fal’s H3 Max and Pika H3 Flex are all post-trains of it. AA also lists Pruna’s P-Video-2-Pro as a MiniMax collaboration. Best for: teams outside excluded regions that want to fine-tune a frontier video model. Seedance 2.5 leads image-to-video. ByteDance began rolling it out on July 31, 2026 through Jimeng AI and Doubao Pro. It supports up to 30-second generations with up to 30 image, 10 video and 10 audio references . Pricing needs care. AA lists $34.12 per minute, the highest on the board. BytePlus lists $1.156 for a 5-second 720p clip without video input , or about $0.23/sec. Confirm API access in your region before planning around it. Best for: reference-heavy, image-led ad and character work. Gemini Omni Flash 1.2 is the newest entry, generally available since November 5, 2026 . It added 3–15 second clips and a 30% price cut over version 1.1. Video output costs $12 per 1M tokens, about $0.070 per second at 720p . It jumped 27 Elo over Omni Flash 1.1 on text-to-video. Requests to 1.1 route to 1.2 from December 3, 2026 . Best for: teams already on the Gemini API who want a top-5 model under $0.11/sec. fal Research post-trained FLUX 3 Max with Black Forest Labs , launching it October 19, 2026. fal says a 10-second 720p clip renders in about 12 seconds . Seedance 2.5 took 277.80 seconds in fal’s own comparison. It shares an API with fal’s H3 Max. Switching between them takes a single model-ID change. Best for: latency-sensitive pipelines and rapid iteration. HeyGen Video 1 is a general scene generator, not an avatar engine. It is a post-train of MiniMax H3 . It leads the silent (audio-off) text-to-video board at 1146 Elo. At $0.04 per second, it costs half of base H3 for a similar score. The API model ID is heygen-video-1 . Best for: high-volume social clips and ad variants where discard rate drives cost. fal Research post-trained H3 Max on the open MiniMax H3 base . It focused on prompt adherence and visual quality. fal claims it renders a 5-second clip in about 3 seconds . It briefly led image-to-video after its August 2026 launch. Newer post-trains have since passed it. Best for: fal users who want H3 quality without self-hosting. SkyReels V4 dates from March 2026 yet still ranks top-5 on image-to-video. At $0.35 per second, it is hard to justify on text-to-video. Gemini Omni Flash 1.2 scores higher for less than a third of the price. FLUX 3 is BFL’s first video model, with 20-second clips and native audio . One backbone also handles robot action prediction. BFL says it will release open-weight versions later this year . Until FLUX 3 Dev ships, treat it as API-only. MiniMax H3 family : Pika H3 Flex shipped October 29, 2026. It cuts H3 to 6 sampling steps . Local inference still needs an H100 80GB and about 215 GB of downloads. Video Rebirth’s HyperFlow H3 Flash compresses H3 to 13.7B. It runs from a 9.1 GB GGUF on a 24 GB GPU. Its sibling, Hyperflow H3, ranks #7 on image-to-video at 1120 Elo. LTX-2.5 : Lightricks released the 22B model on August 11, 2026 . It adds native multishot generation and joint audio. Under the license, entities with $10M+ annual revenue need a paid license . It trails the H3 family by roughly 200 Elo. But it gates by revenue, not territory. For US and EU teams, that makes it a practical default. See our LTX-2.5 launch coverage . Apache 2.0 options : Wan 2.2 and HunyuanVideo 1.5 remain the go-to picks for permissive licensing or a single consumer GPU. Neither appears on the current AA boards. Quality and price no longer track each other. The 3 cheapest top-tier models are all H3 derivatives or H3 itself. Value = (Elo − 1000) ÷ price per second. Higher is better. Illustrative only; it ignores resolution and clip-length differences. At the top, Wan 3.0 buys you about 23 Elo over HeyGen Video 1. It costs 5x more per second. Whether that matters depends on how many takes you discard. The post Best AI Video Generation Models in 2026: Elo, Price per Second, Open Weights appeared first on MarkTechPost .

item.title: Perplexity Releases Decider v1.3: Open-Weight Decision Models Add Locate
item.abstract: Perplexity has released pplx-decider-v1.3 and pplx-decider-flash-v1.3 , the latest versions of its open-weight decision models. Perplexity Decider v1.3 is a decision model that returns probabilities, not generated text. It answers yes/no, multiple-choice and score questions about a text or image input. The main addition is Locate, which extracts exact text spans by type or instruction. Weights ship under Apache 2.0 on Hugging Face . Both models also run in the Perplexity Decisions API and on OpenRouter . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . Decider is Perplexity’s family of decision models, inspired by TypeSafe’s Jev . Each request has a shared ‘state’ plus one or more questions with labeled options. The model returns a probability per option instead of writing an answer. v1.3 succeeds v1.2 and Flash v1.2 . Flash v1.3 is distilled from the large model. Perplexity adapts a generative LLM backbone into a classifier. The output layer starts from the base model’s LM head, pruned to option tokens (A, B, C). A linear decision head reads the hidden state at a <|marker|> token and outputs option probabilities. Full-attention layers are made bidirectional, which Perplexity’s ablations showed helps. v1.3 also changes attention between questions. In v1.2, every question saw every other question, so answers could shift. In v1.3, the state sees all questions, but each question sees only the state and itself. All questions about one input still run in a single forward pass. Weights are averaged across 3 seeds. Flash is trained by minimizing KL divergence to the large model’s outputs. Locate returns exact text spans with start and end character offsets. Fields can be short labels (‘location’) or instructions (‘Extract the city name where the job is located.’). It targets NER, PII detection and extractive QA. A new <|locate|> token is added per requested field. A span head plus a LoRA adapter is trained, while the backbone and decision head stay frozen. The adapter stays unmerged because merging hurt decision accuracy. All results below are self-reported by Perplexity : Benchmark rows are Perplexity’s self-reported numbers from its launch post . The API endpoint is POST https://api.perplexity.ai/v1/decisions . Model IDs are pplx-decider-v1.3 and pplx-decider-flash-v1.3 , with -latest aliases. Pricing is $0.02 and $0.01 per 1M input tokens. Output is free. Perplexity’s latency test put an ~243K-token request at 16s on v1.3 and 5s on Flash. Locate requests allow up to 128 questions. Locally, load the model with Decider.from_pretrained() from the pplx_decider package. Full-attention layers must run noncausally. Perplexity recommends v1.3 for nuanced rubrics and Flash for high-volume routing. Check out the technical details , Decider v1.3 model card , Flash v1.3 model card and API docs . item.title: Export-banned Nvidia chips are behind China’s most powerful AI models — uh-oh, Jensen!
item.abstract: The leading open-weight models developed by Chinese companies were trained on Nvidia chips that the U.S. government restricted from shipping to its largest geopolitical rival, a new research effort claims. The apparently widespread access to Blackwell GPUs among Chinese frontier labs shows the magnitude of the problem facing the leading chip designer. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang left the company this week after admitting to his affair with Alice Huang, executive of Megaspeed, a company implicated in smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Alice Huang has also been alleged to be an agent of China’s intelligence service. While Jensen Huang’s relationships with a customer and two employees have drawn the most public interest, Nvidia’s potential corporate liability for export control violations likely factored into its decision to part ways with Huang. U.S. export controls are intended to protect the country’s leadership in AI capabilities against China, but Huang has long sought to open up that market. Blackwell GPUs are banned from export to China or Chinese-owned firms, while the Trump administration allows Nvidia to export the H200, a less powerful chip, provided shipments take a circuitous shipping route that allows the U.S. to claim a 25% tariff. Will DePue, a former OpenAI researcher who leads the nonprofit research group Unemployment Labs, analyzed the weights — the unique structure — of large language models released openly by DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax, and Ant Group. The weights still reflect the configurations of the chips used to train them, and DePue was able to find compelling evidence that the most closely watched models, including Moonshot’s Kimi’s K3 releases and DeepSeek’s V4 models, bear fingerprints from training on Blackwell chips. White House technology adviser Michael Kratsios said earlier this year that Moonshot had used export-banned Nvidia chips, citing U.S. intelligence sources. Epoch AI, a nonprofit research organization, estimates that about two million advanced chips entered China in 2024 and 2025 through schemes designed to hide their final destination. That doesn’t mean that these models were trained entirely on Nvidia chips, or that export control laws were necessarily violated; the chips could have been in an offshore data center, which has proven a popular way for Chinese firms to access compute and driven an industrial revolution in Malaysia. Epoch’s data estimates that 275,000 Nvidia AI accelerators were imported to Malaysia in 2024 and 2025. However, the ostensible goal of the export bans is to prevent exactly that: Chinese AI labs training on the most powerful chips. China hawks have long called for stronger controls on who uses chips, not just who owns them or where they are installed. “If we care about the U.S. tech edge, it doesn’t make any sense to me that you would not allow Chinese companies to access chips in mainland China or Hong Kong and Macau, but then say, actually, if you just go over to Malaysia, you can do whatever you want,” Sam Bresnick, a researcher at the Georgetown Center for Security and Emerging Technology, told TechCrunch this summer. Megaspeed, the company led by Alice Huang, has been at the center of that trade for several years through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, and has been the subject of investigations by both the U.S. and S i ngaporean government. Friday, Bloomberg also reported that a company with links to Alice Huang was involved in smuggling banned Nvidia chips to a data center in Shanghai. In May, the short-selling research firm Culper published a report arguing that Nvidia had a “ China problem ” because a significant share of its revenue was driven by Chinese demand, either through remote data centers or smuggling in violation of U.S. law. It detailed Megaspeed’s relationship with Nvidia and alleged that Alice Huang’s companies are backed by Chinese firms that are barred from accessing U.S. chips. Ironically, short-seller Culper’s bet against Nvidia wasn’t driven by the expectation of a U.S. government crackdown. Instead, it was focused on the Chinese government’s response to the bans, which was to recommit to its domestic chip industry. If China succeeds, billions of dollars in Chinese demand for Nvidia chips could dry up. Some 600,000 H200 chips are reportedly stockpiled in Hong Kong, awaiting shipment into China. While Chinese companies might want the chips, observers have no consensus on why they haven’t been cleared for import. Graham Webster, a research scholar at Stanford who focuses on U.S.-China technology policy, said he doesn’t buy the idea that holding the chips back would drive domestic production, since demand for chips is so large. Other theories for the hold-up include preparation for a potential trade deal that would involve importing a large volume of U.S. goods, or concerns about potential surveillance technology in the chips. For now, U.S. companies have limited obligations to track what their customers do with controlled goods like AI chips. However, Jensen Huang’s personal and professional entanglements with Alice Huang create a much bigger problem for Nvidia if government investigators confirm that chip smuggling took place and that he was aware of it. Nvidia and Huang have both vouched for Megaspeed’s data centers, saying Nvidia officials had visited them to confirm they were legitimate. The U.S. government’s treatment of Nvidia and Megaspeed is also under scrutiny. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, who oversees the agencies that license chip exports, could reportedly lose his job after reports that his investigators failed to uncover suspicious chip buyers and were too cozy with Nvidia officials.

item.title: Architecture patterns for fast session startup on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime
item.abstract: Agents today review code, process claims, and run unattended for hours. Many also sit behind interactive experiences where a person waits for the first response. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime gives these agents a fully managed, serverless environment: each session runs in its own isolated microVM, the platform scales to zero when there’s no work, and you only pay for the resources your sessions consume. AgentCore runtime with platformVersion set to “V2” changes how sessions start. Instead of initializing your container for every session, it prepares your environment once, snapshots it, and restores that snapshot for each new session. Session start times are faster and more consistent. V2 also reclaims memory your sessions don’t use, so your bill tracks what your agent uses. For most agents, switching to V2 is all it takes. Some agents need restructuring to get the full benefit, and for chat and voice experiences even 2 seconds is too slow. This post explains how V2 starts a session, how to measure session start time, and how to keep work off the first request, including build hooks, which AgentCore runtime now supports. We cover four patterns, from changes to your agent’s code to starting sessions before users need them. AgentCore runtime runs each session in a new microVM. On V1, AgentCore pulls your container image from Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR), starts the container, and runs your initialization code before it can process the first request. The image pull dominates, so cold start grows with image size. V2 does that work once. When you create or update a runtime, AgentCore runtime starts your container in a fresh microVM and waits for the first healthy ping ( GET /ping ), which must arrive within 120 seconds. It then clears the operating system’s file cache, to keep the snapshot small, freezes the microVM, and stores its memory and disk as a snapshot. This is a change from V1: Every create or update now takes a few minutes while the snapshot is built. In this post, init means everything your agent does before /ping reports healthy. With the AgentCore Python SDK, that’s everything before app.run() . If you run your own HTTP server, in Node.js or another language, report healthy only after your initialization finishes. Figure 1: Build, once per create or update When a new session arrives, AgentCore restores the snapshot into a new microVM. Your process resumes exactly where it was frozen, with its imports, objects, and clients in place. Files from your image are loaded lazily: each block is fetched the first time a session reads it. Figure 2: Invoke, every new session Three facts follow from these flows, and the rest of this post builds on them: The following table shows what that means for the work a typical agent does, depending on where it does it: If you know AWS Lambda SnapStart, this will feel familiar. Marc Brooker’s post on how SnapStart loads snapshots and the SnapStart priming strategies post are useful background. Everything in the table assumes your agent can keep what it needs in its own process. That isn’t always possible. A CLI that runs as a separate process and exits, or a browser binary, is read during init and then gone, so a restored session fetches it from the image again. For these cases, you can add a build hook, covered in “Working with hooks.” Figure 3 shows where it runs. Figure 3: Build and invoke with hooks Latency in an agentic application isn’t one number. A request spends time in AgentCore runtime getting a session ready to run your code, then in your code: model calls, tool calls, sub-agents, and streaming the response back. You fix these in different ways, so start by finding out which one dominates. AgentCore runtime publishes both as Amazon CloudWatch metrics in the AWS/Bedrock-AgentCore namespace. Latency is the time to first byte. OverheadLatency is the part that belongs to the platform, such as starting the microVM and restoring the snapshot on a new session. Init doesn’t appear in these metrics because on V2 it runs once, while the snapshot is built, and not in each session. It adds to how long a create or update takes to reach READY, not to request latency. To see how long it takes, log it once before app.run() . The line appears in your runtime’s build logs: Report percentiles such as P90 and P99, or trimmed means such as TM90, which averages the fastest 90% of requests and drops the slowest tail. A plain average hides the slow requests. OverheadLatency covers requests to running sessions as well as new ones, so its distribution depends on how many of your requests start a new session. Compare runs with a similar mix. Test at the rate of new sessions you expect in production, not with a handful of sessions after a deploy. To include network time from your client, measure on the client as well. Time the invoke call, have your handler return how long it ran, and subtract. Both timestamps come from the same machine, so clock differences between the client and the microVM don’t matter. If you stream, very small events can be held back until a few hundred bytes of output build up, so time to first event can read higher than session start. The usual cold start advice is to import lazily and keep initialization small. On V2, do the opposite: init runs once, when the snapshot is built, and work deferred to the handler is paid by every new session. This applies to static work: imports, clients, and data from your image. Dynamic data can’t be snapshotted. The next section covers it. The agents that notice most are the ones that read large files from their image at request time: weights for a small local model, embeddings, datasets, large libraries, a browser binary for automation, or a CLI toolchain that a coding agent runs as subprocesses. Reading many small files, as compiling a TypeScript project does, has the same effect. An agent that imports a few libraries and calls a hosted model mostly needs to get its imports and clients right. Create objects during init, not only imports. Creating an object loads the modules it depends on and keeps them in active memory. Initialize local tools that use external libraries during init too, not when the agent first calls them. Create your clients during init. Endpoint resolution, credential resolution, and the client’s modules all come back with the snapshot. Sockets don’t, but boto3 clients reconnect cleanly on the first call. Some other network clients first try the stale socket, which adds hundreds of milliseconds, so close their connections before the snapshot. Keep static data in memory, such as prompts, skill front matter, configuration, and small indexes. Hold the data in an object, not only a read of it: Keep tools running instead of starting them per request. A subprocess launched in the handler reads its binary and libraries from the image in every new session. A long-running helper started during init, such as a language server or a worker process with its imports done, comes back as part of process memory. Talk to it over a pipe or socket. Copy files you can’t hold in memory to a RAM-backed disk. Toolchains like tsc run as separate programs that read their own files. Copy them to /dev/shm or a ramfs mount during init so their reads come from memory. Ship compiled bytecode. uv pip install doesn’t compile by default, so late imports also compile from source. Set UV_COMPILE_BYTECODE=1 or use pip install --compile . The example below builds the agent, its model, and its clients during init, so every session inherits them: The trade-off: time to first byte on a new session is the time to start the microVM and restore the snapshot, plus the time your handler takes. Moving work into init shortens the handler, but anything you hold in memory makes the snapshot larger. You also pay for that held memory in every session.

item.abstract: Foundation models deployed on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod meet inputs that no pre-curated dataset covers: domain-specific jargon, unexpected formats, new products, and changing user behavior. Without a record of production inference data, teams can’t detect drift, find failure patterns, or use real interactions to improve the model. Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now provides Data Capture, a built-in capability that records live inference inputs and outputs to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) at three independent tiers, with minimal latency impact and zero impact on model availability. In this post, we walk through one complete example on a single SageMaker HyperPod cluster. A home-appliance support router captures its production traffic, Amazon Athena queries surface a new-product blind spot, a SQL policy labels the captured records, and a fine-tune on that data teaches the router the new product. We measure accuracy before and after, on data that could not have existed before the model was deployed. The inference operator serves the model on one node, and the training operator runs the fine-tuning on another. We use synthetic data for the walkthrough. The scripts, manifests, SQL, synthetic datasets, and expected outputs are available in the accompanying GitHub repository . HyperPod Data Capture provides three independent tiers, each at a different point in the request path. You can turn on any combination in the same dataCapture block. Tiers 1 and 3 both store full payloads, so enabling both stores every record twice. Use Tier 1 for compliance and Model Monitor, Tier 2 when you only need traffic metadata, and Tier 3 when you intend to use the payloads. This post uses Tier 3 only. Because Tier 3 records complete payloads, which can include names, addresses, and order numbers, protect that data before it becomes training data. Use sampling, AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption ( kmsKeyId ), S3 lifecycle rules, and personally identifiable information (PII) redaction (for example, with Amazon Comprehend). Figure 1: The five-step flywheel on a single SageMaker HyperPod cluster, from capture through Athena analysis, labeling, fine-tuning, and redeploy The inference operator adds three sidecars to the model pod. Every request that passes through the NGINX proxy is copied to an OpenTelemetry collector, batched, and written to S3 through a Mountpoint-S3 volume. Athena reads those files in place. The training operator runs the fine-tune as a HyperPodPyTorchJob on a second GPU, and the new model is served by a second endpoint that also has capture on. Every later step reads these. For the policy statements, see Data capture for inference on HyperPod . The next three steps deploy the router with Tier 3 capture on, check that the pod runs the capture sidecars, and confirm that records reach Amazon S3. This is the whole feature: the dataCapture.modelPod.enabled: true block. Everything else is an ordinary vLLM deployment. The preceding modelPod block sets 100% sampling and captures both input and output, which are the defaults. The model container and the pod’s app label are both named after modelName . In our run, the pod was ready about five minutes after kubectl apply , most of it spent downloading the weights. item.title: Faster Scientific Simulations with New FP64 Algorithms in NVIDIA cuBLAS
item.abstract: Many scientific simulations, from molecular chemistry to materials science, spend the majority of their execution time computing high-precision dense general matrix multiplications (GEMM). These operations are called DGEMM for real 64-bit floating-point numbers and ZGEMM for complex 64-bit floating-point numbers. cuBLAS is widely used by HPC and AI applications to accelerate GEMM and other Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms (BLAS) on NVIDIA GPUs. Rapid advances in lower-precision hardware have motivated exploration of a new class of algorithms that deliver full double-precision results on the faster integer Tensor Cores. With CUDA Toolkit 13.4.2, cuBLAS no longer has to choose between accuracy and speed. cuBLAS breaks each double-precision number into integer pieces, multiplies them on the GPU’s Tensor Cores, and reassembles the exact result. The answers keep full double-precision accuracy, but the work runs on faster hardware. Two new algorithms make this more efficient: Ozaki-II needs fewer integer multiplications than the earlier Ozaki-I approach, and the 2M method cuts a complex matrix multiplication from four real multiplications to two. This builds on the Automatic Dynamic Precision (ADP) framework introduced in Unlocking Tensor Core Performance with Floating Point Emulation in cuBLAS , which delivers higher double-precision (FP64) matrix-multiplication performance by mapping FP64 arithmetic onto integer Tensor Cores while preserving native FP64 accuracy. cuBLAS delivers automatic acceleration of DGEMM and ZGEMM with no application code changes. Because speed matters only when accuracy is not compromised, we validate both on real-world applications: coupled cluster singles and doubles (CCSD) in quantum chemistry, and BerkeleyGW in materials science. This post explains how the algorithms work, shows benchmark and application results, and covers how to get started. Performance highlights cuBLAS in CUDA Toolkit 13.4.2 delivers the following performance gains: cuBLAS DGEMM with Ozaki-II runs 5.5x and 3.9x faster than native FP64 on NVIDIA VR NVL72 and NVIDIA GB200, respectively. It’s also 2x faster than Ozaki-I on NVIDIA GB200. CCSD case study using cuBLAS DGEMM with Ozaki-II achieves 2x and 1.4x end-to-end speedup over native FP64 on NVIDIA VR NVL72 and NVIDIA GB200 in FP64. In domain-specific mixed-precision mode, end-to-end speedup over native FP64 is 5x and 3.5x on NVIDIA VR NVL72 and NVIDIA GB200 respectively. cuBLAS ZGEMM with 2M algorithm achieves a 5x speedup over native Complex FP64 (CFP64) on NVIDIA GB200. BerkeleyGW case study using cuBLAS ZGEMM with 2M algorithm achieves 6.6x and 3.9x speedup over native ZGEMM on NVIDIA VR NVL72 and NVIDIA GB200 respectively. cuBLAS DGEMM with Ozaki-II achieves up to 175, 147, and 37 TFLOPS on NVIDIA VR NVL72, NVIDIA GB200, NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 respectively. From Ozaki-I to Ozaki-II Ozaki-I and Ozaki-II schemes share a common first step, but differ in how the big integer multiplication is performed. Both the schemes align the exponents of the input matrices and convert them to a shared-exponent, variable-length integer representation so that products accumulate exactly on integer Tensor Cores. cuBLAS uses heuristics to automatically choose between Ozaki-I and Ozaki-II for best performance. The integer width is chosen by ADP at runtime or can also be set explicitly by the user. Ozaki-I breaks each big integer into 8-bit slices and multiplies slices of A against slices of B in a triangular pattern, so the number of Tensor Core GEMMs grows with the square of the slice count. Ozaki-II uses a faster big-integer multiplication algorithm based on the Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT). It reduces each quantized operand modulo a set of small pairwise-coprime integers, performs exactly one integer GEMM per modulus, and reconstructs the exact product from the residues. With Ozaki-II, the GEMM count is linear in the number of moduli, whereas Ozaki-I grows with the square of the slice count, so the advantage widens as the accuracy target rises. At the accuracy required to match FP64, Ozaki-I needs roughly twice as many Tensor Core GEMMs as Ozaki-II. Because Ozaki-II materializes one residue pair per modulus, a naive implementation would carry a much larger workspace than Ozaki-I. However, cuBLAS already applies the memory-parsimonious tiling introduced for Ozaki-I in CTK 13.3 to Ozaki-II scheme as well, discarding each residue pair immediately after its GEMM. This results in a more manageable workspace size. cuBLAS ADP framework is designed to provide accuracy guarantees comparable to, or better than, standard floating-point GEMM algorithms. More information on the accuracy of fixed-point methods can be found in the references. If at run-time, the number of mantissa bits required to preserve FP64-equivalent accuracy exceeds the library default or a user-supplied maximum, cuBLAS falls-back to a code path that utilizes the native FP64 MMA instructions. So, applications can safely use cuBLAS in their production deployments without worrying about numerical accuracy. Figure 1, below, shows the speedup of cuBLAS DGEMM using Ozaki-II over Ozaki-I on GB200. DGEMM performance Figure 1. Speedup of DGEMM with Ozaki-II scheme in cuBLAS shipped with CTK 13.4.2 over the Ozaki-I scheme in CTK 13.3.1 on GB200 NVIDIA Rubin Rubin introduces a new numeric format, TI16 (12-bit integer in sign-magnitude format with range of [-2047, +2047]), that is aptly suited for the acceleration of Ozaki scheme computations. cuBLAS 13.4 uses TI16 type for acceleration of Ozaki-I and Ozaki-II computations through the tcgen05.mma instruction on NVIDIA Rubin GPUs (compute capability 10.7). Figure 2, below, shows the speedup of cuBLAS DGEMM using Ozaki-II over native FP64 on VR NVL72. Figure 2. Speedup of DGEMM with Ozaki-II scheme over native FP64 on VR NVL72 DGEMM application performance – CCSD in quantum chemistry To demonstrate the potential application performance of Ozaki-II DGEMM, we consider the use case of coupled cluster singles and doubles (CCSD). CCSD is a foundational post-DFT method in electronic structure that together with the (T) perturbative correction (not considered here) forms the “gold standard” of quantum chemistry. Moreover, the response of CCSD to various perturbations yields the EOM-CCSD treatment of electronic excited states and the CCSD lambda treatment of property computations. CCSD is noteworthy for its very high cost of dense FP64 tensor contractions, which the Ozaki-II scheme in cuBLAS can significantly accelerate. A small CCSD demonstration was implemented using cuBLAS in CTK 13.4.2 for the main tensor contractions, with the coupled cluster problem setup accelerated by cuEST v0.2.2. A standard FP64 single-GPU T1-transformed restricted CCSD approach was constructed in the density fitting representation. Figure 3, below, shows performance data for frozen-core CCSD/cc-pVTZ for five mid-sized members of the S22 database — these systems contain 24–28 atoms and roughly 590–630 atomic orbitals. Ozaki-II DGEMM with ESC guaranteeing full FP64 precision causes performance to rise monotonically with generation, yielding a total speedup of 4.7x of Rubin over A100. Another compelling possibility is to use an application-specific mixed precision mode with a fixed Ozaki-II mantissa bit budget, here selected to be 32 mantissa bits. This also yields monotonic performance gains, with total speedup now at 11.5x native FP64 A100. With ESC at full FP64 quality, results are indistinguishable from native FP64 precision – errors in the CCSD correlation energy are <10 -14 E h . Ozaki-II emulation provides the opportunity to use lower fixed precision with 32 mantissa bits while still providing sufficient accuracy for the vast majority of practical applications; errors in the energy are <10 -10 E h and the amplitude equations can be converged to a residual of 10 -9 or better.
