item.title: Adapt Human Motion for Robots with NVIDIA SOMA Retargeter
item.abstract: Human motion offers roboticists a great starting point for teaching humanoid robots how to move. A human demonstration captures the coordination and timing behind natural movement, from everyday actions to complex tasks. But a robot cannot simply copy the same joint motion from a human. Its proportions, joint structure, and range of motion are different, so the movement needs to be adapted to fit the robot. The open source NVIDIA SOMA Retargeter helps you adapt human motion to your robot’s proportions and range of motion. Built around the shared human-motion representation in NVIDIA SOMA-X , it provides tools to configure your robot, refine the resulting movement, and process motion data for downstream training. This post explains the retargeting process, the tools for refining robot motion, and the connection to policy learning. From human motion to robot joint trajectories Human motion can come from many sources, including a motion capture session, a video, an online dataset, or a generative model. These sources often output motion with different skeletons and file formats. Representing compatible human motion on the SOMA skeleton gives the retargeter a consistent input. SOMA Retargeter reads a Biovision Hierarchy (BVH) animation on the SOMA base skeleton. As Figure 1 below shows, it scales motion targets to the robot’s proportions, solves for joint poses, and applies configured corrections. The output is a comma-separated values (CSV) file containing the robot’s root position, orientation, and joint angles for each frame. These trajectories describe the desired movement for a downstream learning or control system. Figure 1. The retargeting pipeline converts SOMA BVH motion into robot joint trajectories through scaling, inverse kinematics, and post-processing. Across many clips, the resulting animations can form a motion library for downstream reference preparation and policy training. Sources of human motion Developers can draw on recorded performances, reconstruct motion from video, or generate new movements: Motion-capture data. BONES-SEED provides a collection of human motion-capture data. Video reconstruction. GEM-X reconstructs whole-body 3D human motion from a single video using the SOMA body model. Its demo workflow connects video reconstruction with G1 retargeting, showing how a recorded action can become a robot motion reference. Motion generation. Kimodo and ARDY let developers generate human movement from text and pose constraints. Kimodo supports creating motion sequences from those descriptions, while ARDY adds interactive steering as the motion unfolds. Both offer models that generate motion on the SOMA skeleton. Adapting motion to different humanoid robots The SOMA Retargeter v0.2 release includes sample motions supplied by Bones from the BONES-SEED dataset, along with reference retargeting results and configurations for five humanoid robots: Unitree G1 , Unitree H2 , Booster T1, AgiBot X2 Ultra , and AgiBot A3T3 . These examples show how joint angles and foot placement change across humanoid embodiments according to their specific proportions and range of motion. The paired human motions and robot results give you a starting point for exploring the tool and comparing your own output. For this example, use the supplied Unitree G1 configuration to retarget a forward walk from the sample motions. After installing SOMA Retargeter , open a terminal in the repository root and start the viewer: uv run python app/bvh_to_csv_converter.py --config assets/default_bvh_to_csv_converter_config.json --viewer gl The BVH to CSV Converter opens with unitree_g1 selected by default. In Scene Options, expand Motion, select Load on the BVH Motion row, and open the bundled file from here . The SOMA human animation appears in the viewer. Under Scene Options → Motion, select Retarget on the BVH Motion row. The retargeter scales the source targets to G1, solves the configured inverse-kinematics objectives for each frame, and applies the configured post-processing. The viewer then displays the robot animation with the human source motion. Positioning gizmos let you separate them for inspection. Figure 2 . The BVH to CSV Converter displays the human source motion alongside the retargeted Unitree G1 motion, with controls for loading, retargeting, and saving the result. Use the playback controls to inspect the result. A recognizable forward walk and continuous motion are useful first checks; the robot’s poses will differ from the human’s because its proportions and joints are different. Under CSV Motion, select Save and give the output a new name, such as my_first_retarget.csv, to keep it separate from the supplied reference. The saved file contains the robot’s root pose and joint values over the animation. To compare your output with the supplied G1 reference result for this walk, use the CSV Motion Load control to open each CSV in turn and inspect the same point in the motion. The reference file is located in the repository here . The results should show the same general movement, though exact values can vary with configuration and dependency versions. The first-retarget guide covers this example in more detail. Configuring your robot and refining its motion The supplied G1 configuration gives you a starting point for retargeting, while the included reference result provides a point of comparison as you adjust the settings to refine the motion. With the Robot Configurator , you can refine an existing robot configuration or create one for a new robot by loading its robot description and defining how human motion maps to it. You can align human and robot reference poses, adjust scale, and map the source skeleton to robot body parts. The resulting configuration can be saved and reused across motion clips. Figure 3. The source motion is a one-handed wave, but an unaligned reference pose makes Booster T1 hold both arms outward (left). After aligning the robot’s reference pose with the SOMA human reference, one hand waves beside its head while the other arm rests at its side (right). Both panels use the same input motion and IK settings, isolating the effect of reference-pose alignment. The retargeting solver uses inverse kinematics (IK) from Newton , built with NVIDIA Warp , to find joint poses that follow the scaled human targets. When a robot cannot match every target at once, IK weights determine which body parts take priority. The experimental IK weight optimizer tunes these weights using a small set of motions representative of the robot’s intended tasks. It tests weight adjustments by retargeting those motions and checking how closely and smoothly the robot follows the targets. The selected weights are saved in a new retargeting configuration. Sliding feet can introduce conflicting targets for a downstream motion-tracking policy: the reference foot moves while the intended action calls for planted contact. Foot-plant correction addresses this artifact by adjusting foot motion during detected contact intervals. You can refine contact timing and correction settings to reduce sliding in the reference motion before it enters a training pipeline. Once you have refined a configuration on representative motions, headless batch retargeting lets you reuse it across a larger collection for your target robot, without operating the viewer for each clip. Using retargeted motion to train robot policies During training, a motion-tracking policy learns how to turn the retargeted reference into control actions, using both the desired motion and the robot’s current state. The SONIC training workflow includes a SOMA CSV converter for G1 . It converts retargeted trajectories into SONIC’s motion-library format for training. ProtoMotions offers another framework for physics-based motion tracking. In either case, the input representation and policy need to match the target robot.

item.title: Brave Search API now accepts agentic payments via the x402 protocol
item.abstract:
The Brave Search API , our developer tool for building applications with data from the Web, is adding support for instant, pay-as-you-go, agentic payments enabled by the open x402 payment protocol. Developers and autonomous AI agents that specifically require agentic search can now programmatically query Brave’s independent search index, ground agent responses, and settle requests in real time, which eliminates the need for traditional API key management. Integrating x402 with the Brave Search API makes it easier for an agentic harness to leverage Brave Search API via a CLI wallet, as Brave runs its own facilitator accepting USDC on the Base blockchain, with acceptance on other networks and with other stablecoins incoming soon. This allows a Brave Search API user the ability to pay for LLM Context (agentic grounding) or general web search on-demand, without first creating an account and selecting a plan. Instead, simply transfer USDC stablecoin to your agent’s wallet via the Base network and it’s ready to access the same high-quality search results powered by Brave’s search engine. How does it work? Brave Search API endpoints behind x402 require payment on every request rather than authentication. A request sent without payment receives an HTTP 402 Payment Required response that states the price of that search and the payment details needed to pay it. The agent signs a USDC payment for that amount and retries the request with the signed payment attached. Once the payment is verified, the search runs and results are returned with a receipt of the transaction that occurred on the Base blockchain. Get started today Pricing follows Brave’s published API rates: LLM Context, an API designed specifically for providing search context for agents, will cost $0.005 ($5 per 1,000). Additionally, web (search for humans), news, image, video, and local endpoints will also be available for $0.005 ($5 per 1,000). Gas fees for transacting on the Base blockchain will be covered for a limited time. Since each request carries its own payment, a Brave Search API account is no longer needed to use the service. The easiest path to query via x402 is to install Purl Wallet, a Stripe-developed CLI wallet for your agent. Set up your wallet, top it off using Base-native USDC, and start querying today. Ready to build pay-as-you-go search into your apps or AI agents? Check out our Brave Search x402 Proxy Documentation and explore: https://api-dashboard.search.brave.com/documentation/guides/agent-payments

item.abstract: AI News Tech ChatGPT Wallet lets OpenAI’s Dots agents make purchases for you OpenAI says ChatGPT Wallet won’t share your actual credit card info with its AI agents.﻿ OpenAI says ChatGPT Wallet won’t share your actual credit card info with its AI agents.﻿ by Stevie Bonifield Nov 13, 2026, 8:45 PM UTC Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images Stevie Bonifield is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI. After launching its Dots AI agents platform earlier this year, OpenAI is launching a wallet for the agents. ChatGPT Wallet is rolling out starting today for ChatGPT Pro subscribers in the US aged 18 and older using a US billing address and “eligible US-issued American Express, Chase, Mastercard and Visa cards.” After adding a card to the wallet, your Dots agents can use it to buy things in response to your prompts, but they’ll check in with you each time before checking out. Users have to approve every purchase from ChatGPT Wallet. Image: OpenAI After you review the AI agent’s purchase and sign off on it, OpenAI says that, similar to using tap to pay , Apple Pay , or Google Wallet , it substitutes your credit card details with a payment token, so your actual card info isn’t shared with your Dots agent or the business you’re buying from. Eventually, OpenAI says it expects “users to be able to delegate purchases entirely to their agent by setting clear parameters—such as spending limits, purchase categories, or time periods—and pre-approve those purchases.” ChatGPT Wallet might not work everywhere. Some retailers have restrictions on AI agents or block them altogether. Earlier this year, Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse agents.
